note: Batch 1 broad survey of base feature families across lookbacks to map which raw factors carry cross-sectional signal
Batch 2 map lookback term structure of the volatility and beta risk-premium families and the sign-flipped reversal family
Batch 3 optimize risk-premium composites at long lookbacks and test whether reversal adds orthogonal value on top

text: Approach. Batch 1 was a broad sweep of every base feature family across the lookback grid to find which raw factors carry cross-sectional signal, rather than starting from a guessed alpha. Two dominant and independent structures appeared. First, a risk-premium block: std and beta both load positively and their term structures are smooth and monotone increasing in lookback (std 20 to 250 goes 1.11, 1.18, 1.37, 1.57, 1.66; beta 20 to 250 goes 0.68, 0.73, 0.97, 1.25, 1.42). Monotonicity across a parameter grid is my main guard against overfitting - a single lucky lookback would show a spike, not a ramp. Second, a reversal block: ret(10) and maxr load negatively, ma loads positively, all consistent with buying recent losers. Batch 3 confirmed the two blocks are close to orthogonal: equal-weight cs_z of std(250) and beta(250) gives 1.58, and adding a cs_z reversal leg lifts it to 1.92, which is far more than a redundant leg would add. Plan from here is to optimize the composite weighting, hunt for a genuine third family (skew, kurt, range position) rather than another repackaging of the same two blocks, and then stress the finalists for parameter robustness and signal-decay sensitivity before reporting. I will deliberately avoid reporting three near-identical variants of one composite, since that concentrates all OOS risk on a single regime bet on high-volatility high-beta assets continuing to outperform.

Batch 5 parameter perturbation of the leading composite plus wider multi-leg builds to test whether the 2.0 plateau is a robust ridge or a narrow peak

text: Final selection logic. The panel contains one dominant multi-block structure, not a single alpha. Five roughly independent blocks pay: (1) a risk premium in which high long-horizon volatility and high beta outperform, with smooth monotone term structures rising from 20 to 250 days; (2) short-horizon reversal at about 10 days, corroborated broadly by maxr across every window from 10 to 120 and by ma, so the block is real even though the ret lookback itself peaks sharply at 10; (3) short-window return skewness, positive and stable across 5 to 20 days; (4) kurtosis and a vol-expansion term, ts_z of std(120) over 250; (5) long-horizon momentum at 250 days plus range position. Equal-weight cross-sectional z-scores of legs drawn from all five blocks compound well: two legs give about 1.6, four give about 2.0, eight give about 2.4, and twelve to fifteen give 2.55 to 2.73. Breadth is doing the work, which is the outcome I trust most out of sample because it is estimation-error reduction rather than parameter selection. Overfitting controls applied. Leave-one-out on the fourteen leg ensemble moves SR only between 2.55 and 2.73, so no single leg carries it, and notably dropping either std(250) or beta(250) slightly raises SR, confirming those two are mutually redundant rather than individually critical. Adding an arbitrary thirteenth leg lands anywhere in 2.39 to 2.69, so the local noise band is roughly plus or minus 0.15 and any ranking inside the plateau is meaningless. I therefore did not report the raw argmax. I chose three points near the top of the plateau on BOTH SR and rank IC, preferring high IC where SR was tied, because a variant with high SR but depressed IC is earning its Sharpe from lower realised volatility rather than better prediction and is less likely to persist. The three differ in the construction of the reversal leg, which leave-one-out identified as the highest-attribution single block, and in ensemble breadth, so a failure of any one parameter choice does not take down all three. I deliberately stopped with a batch unused, since further search inside a flat plateau would only be mining noise.

rationale: Three wide equal-weight cross-sectional z-score ensembles spanning five independent blocks found in the panel: long-horizon volatility and beta risk premium, short-horizon reversal, short-window return skewness, kurtosis and vol expansion, and long-horizon momentum with range position. Train SR 2.69, 2.68 and 2.68 with rank IC 0.0166, 0.0172 and 0.0165. Selection was driven by robustness rather than by the raw train argmax: every base block has a smooth monotone or broad lookback term structure, leave-one-out moves SR only within 2.55 to 2.73 so no single leg carries the result, and swapping an arbitrary marginal leg spans plus or minus 0.15, meaning ranking inside the plateau is noise. I picked points strong on both SR and IC, favouring IC on ties since Sharpe earned through low realised volatility rather than prediction is less likely to persist. The three vary the reversal construction, which leave-one-out flagged as the highest attribution block, and vary ensemble breadth, so no single parameter choice can take down all three.
